question.problem:
Fill in the blanks to make the following reasoning true.

Since $\text{gcd}(62,77)=$
{{field-1}}, 
by the extended Euclidean algorithm, we have 

| $1\,=\,62\,\cdot ($
{{field-2}}
$)+\,77\,\cdot ($
{{field-3}}

Therefore, ${62}^{-1}\,\text{mod}\,77=$
{{field-4}} (expressed as the smallest nonnegative residue).
question.worked_solution:
First of all, notice that $\text{gcd}(62,77)=1.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $62$ modulo $77$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $62$ modulo $77$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
62\cdot x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,77).
$$

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}77 & = & 62\cdot 1 & + & 15 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 62 & = & 15\cdot 4 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 15 & = & 2\cdot 7 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =77-62 \\ 2 & =62-15\cdot 4 \\ 1 & =15-2\cdot 7.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =15-2\cdot 7 \\  & =15-(62-15\cdot 4)\cdot 7 \\  & =15-62\cdot 7+15\cdot 28 \\  & =15\cdot 29-62\cdot 7 \\  & =(77-62)\cdot 29-62\cdot 7 \\  & =77\cdot 29-62\cdot 29-62\cdot 7 \\  & =62\cdot (-36)+77\cdot 29\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result modulo $77,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}62\cdot (-36)+77\cdot 29 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,77) \\ 62\cdot (-36) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,77) \\ 62\cdot (77-36) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,77) \\ 62\cdot 41 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,77)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $62\cdot 41≡1\,(\text{mod}\,77),$ which means that ${62}^{-1}\,\text{mod}\,77=41.$
